_comment: Campaign level index (LEVELS.md).
20 levels across three markets: 9 international (us_equity), 9 indian
(india_equity), 2 crypto. GameStop is LEVELS.md's optional 10th
international slot and is marked needs_decision, not defaulted in.
data_status - does the level have real data files?
sourced        - <id>.json and <id>_script.json exist and are real
pending_source - no data yet
needs_decision - a product/spec question must be answered first
licence - is that data cleared to SHIP? These are independent.
cleared    - redistribution in a published app is permitted
unverified - the level plays, but publishing it is not cleared
NOTHING is 'cleared' yet. Equity levels come from Yahoo (terms forbid
redistribution) and index levels are the provider's IP. Crypto comes from
Binance's public market data, whose terms still need a read. All levels
are playable for development and demo; none are clear to publish.
Swapping to a licensed vendor is a change to the importer's fetch step.
reveal_title is shown ONLY after a level has been cleared. Blind mode
(ENGINE.md 3) is worthless if the map names the crash before you play it.
Prices, dates and optimal_action are computed by tool/import_*.dart from
the real series. None are typed by hand.

levels.description: On 19 October 1987 world markets fell further in a single session than on any day before or since. There was no bankruptcy, no war, no obvious trigger — computerised programme trading and portfolio insurance turned an ordinary decline into a rout, with each wave of selling forcing the next. The index regained its pre-crash level within about two years.

levels.open_question: Intraday event. On the 1D timeframe the app commits to (ENGINE.md 7, DESIGN.md) this is a single bar with no drawdown to survive, so it needs intraday OHLCV — the one level in the set that does.
levels.description: On 6 May 2010 US markets collapsed and substantially recovered inside a single afternoon. Liquidity briefly vanished and some shares traded at absurd prices before the move reversed. It is a test of reacting to velocity rather than to a lasting change in value.

The internet boom ended slowly rather than all at once. From March 2000 the Nasdaq ground downwards for roughly two and a half years, with repeated convincing rallies along the way. Companies with no earnings went to zero; some of the survivors became the largest firms on earth. The hard part was that you could watch it coming, day after day.

In mid-2013 the US Federal Reserve signalled it would slow the bond buying that had supported markets since the financial crisis. Nothing had actually changed in the economy — only the expectation of future support. The selloff was sharp but comparatively mild, which is exactly what makes it a fair test when you cannot see the label.

In August 2011 a political standoff over the US borrowing limit ended with the country losing its top credit rating for the first time. The fall was fast and driven by politics rather than by company earnings.

Slowing Chinese growth and a surprise currency move spilled into global markets from August 2015. It arrived as two distinct waves months apart, so a recovery that looked like the end was only half of it.

The collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 turned a housing downturn into a global financial crisis. Banks stopped trusting each other, credit froze, and the decline ran for months rather than days before bottoming in March 2009. This is the flagship international level: long, relentless, and full of false dawns.

In February and March 2020 markets priced in a global pandemic faster than almost any decline in history — and then recovered faster too. Almost everyone playing this lived through it, which makes it the clearest demonstration of how differently a crash reads from inside it.

In March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failed after a deposit run, taking other regional lenders with it. The shock was sharp, sector-specific and quickly contained — a test of whether you panic at alarming news that turns out not to be systemic.

levels.open_question: LEVELS.md's optional 10th international slot, flagged rather than defaulted in. It is a bubble, not a crash: the disciplined move was arguably not chasing euphoria, which does not fit the hold-vs-panic-sell mould the scoring assumes. Include only with bespoke script and reveal copy.
levels.description: In early 2021 a crowd of retail traders drove GameStop to extraordinary levels, squeezing funds that had bet against it. This is a bubble, not a crash: the disciplined move was arguably never to chase it at all, which is why it does not fit the same scoring mould as every other level.

In April 1992 India learned that a stockbroker had funnelled money out of the banking system to inflate share prices. The market fell hard when the scam broke and kept falling for the following year. It remains India's most iconic market scandal.
On 17 May 2004 an unexpected election result raised doubts about whether economic reform would continue. The Sensex fell so fast that trading was halted. A political shock, not an economic one.

India's own dot-com bubble, inflated by a broker borrowing heavily against the shares he was buying. When it unwound in 2001 the market ground down for months. A different story from Harshad Mehta despite the surface similarity.

Through 2007 the Indian market suffered sharp single-day falls that felt like the beginning of something larger — and were not. The real crisis arrived the following year. This is a level about not spending your nerve on the false alarm.
China's currency devaluation in August 2015 hit Indian equities as part of a global risk-off move. The same trigger as the international China-led selloff, seen from a different market.

On 8 November 2016 India withdrew its two largest banknotes overnight. The market fell over the following days on a purely domestic policy shock — the one event in this set with no global cause at all.

levels.reveal_title: 2008 — The Global Financial Crisis in India
levels.description: The global financial crisis reached India through foreign investors pulling money out rather than through failing Indian banks. The Sensex fell further than most Western indices. Pairs with the international 2008 level as the same crisis seen from two markets.

levels.reveal_title: March 2020 — The COVID Crash in India
levels.description: India's pandemic crash was steeper than the international version and recovered even faster, compressed further by a nationwide lockdown announced mid-fall.

levels.open_question: LEVELS.md leaves this open. Candidates: the 2013 rupee-crisis-adjacent selloff, or a further-verified 2025 tariff-shock event (which LEVELS.md separately flags as high scrutiny — very recent and politically live). Pick one or drop the slot.
levels.description: Reserved for a second India-specific event. Not yet chosen.

After peaking in December 2017, Bitcoin spent all of 2018 falling. There was no single catastrophe — just a slow, grinding unwind of a speculative mania, punctuated by rallies that each looked like the bottom. It ties directly into the Daily Pivot's crypto theme.

In May 2022 the Terra/LUNA stablecoin collapsed, and in November the FTX exchange failed with customer funds missing. Unlike 2018 this was driven by fraud and contagion rather than a broad speculative unwind — the danger was counterparties, not valuations.
